rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Build 4 Sail 5 Deliver 6 Trade 7 Emperor's Visit 8 Game End Overview Move your ships, please customers, and construct buildings to have the most points over 2 Eras Turn At the start of your turn, you may choose to spend Divine Favor in order to change your dice value by 1 up or down, your sun value is how much divine favor you have whilst your moon value is the maximum you can currently hold After which, you can take an action between: Build, Sail, or Deliver Thirdly, if able you're allowed to claim Masteries, these are shared goals with the first person to complete them gaining more points than later claimants. You can claim as many Masteries as you currently satisfy, but can only claim each unique Mastery once. Finally, roll your dice in preparation for next turn Note: You can only hold 25 Koku and 6 copies of each trade good at any one point Build Pick an empty shore space which matches the icon on the dice Pay the Koku cost displayed there, if you cannot pay it then you cannot build there Take a building tile of your choice and add it to the space, if you take the tile at the end of the row then you get a bonus of 1 Divine Favor Place one of your Clan Markers on it and move your Influence marker for the corresponding region the number of spaces depicted on the building bonus. (The rose shown on each influence track refers specifically to one of masteries so won't be relevant in games without that mastery in play) Gain any rewards from the influence track if you pass or land on them Add a new tile into the building row and slide all the others along, if this was the last tile from Era 1 then it will trigger Emperor's Visit (see below) Sail Pick a single ship of yours and move it downriver by the value of your dice Each river space is connected to 4 building spaces Gain the rewards shown of the point, an empty space always gives 1 Koku, whilst the built structures have various rewards The owners of any buildings you just gathered from also gain the reward shown on the flat end of the tile, furthest from the river, if you own a building you gathered from you gain both rewards If the owner reward is Influence, it is the track associated with the region the building is based at If your ship just reached the end of the river, gain either 3 Koku or 1 Trade Good, discard the building tile at the end of the building row (This may cause an Emperor's Visit), then put the ship back at the start of the river and complete any further movement points you still have Deliver Pick a card in your hand which has a dice symbol matching the dice you hold Discard the Trade Goods in its request area (Dark banner under name) If you can't satisfy either of these first two steps, then you cannot take this action Place the card in your playing area A Tick reward is gained immediately A cycled reward is an ongoing benefit A cup reward is an end game effect The Monk's Moon symbol will increase your divine favour capacity by 1. Draw 2 new cards, then discard 1 from your hand (which can be an old one or one just drawn) Trade At any time you may Trade: Exchange two of the same Trade Good for one of any other Trade Good. Exchange five Koku to gain one Divine Favor. Emperor's Visit When the last building tile from Era I is moved into the available supply for the first time, this triggers a Visit after the current player has finished their turn All players gain the ownership reward of their buildings the same way as if a ship had visited After which, place the Era 2 deck into play and continue Game End This is triggered similar to the Emperor's Visit, but when Era 2 deck is depleted The player who triggered it scores 5 points, then each other player gets a bonus turn Score each Influence region by rank, 1st ahead, 2nd ahead, and 3rd ahead where applicable, if you are not on a track you cannot score a rank. If tied, the tied players add their ranks together and divide evenly, with the excess points ignored. Customers have two scoring parts First, score customers with any end game scoring conditions Secondly, score customers simply by how many you obtained Customers 1 2 3 4 5 6+ Score 2 5 9 14 20 27 Add to this any Mastery rewards obtained during the game The player with the most points, wins! If tied, the player with the most remaining Divine Favor wins!

[Rating: 2/10] I like how simply the game plays, but it is all over the place in an unpleasant way that many modern euros tend to be. You can move on the track, or you can play the deliver mini-game, but don't forget about the race for the goals mini-game. My eyes are bouncing all over and it's icon soup the whole time. This is really just a low interaction resource conversion euro disguised as a some-for-you-some-for-me interactive game. The random cards are just bad. [Rating: 3/10] Bursting with too much of all the things, but not enough gold to plaster over the resulting cracks. The pleasantly simple and straightforward core loop is ruined by being tacked on a generous helping of all the mechanisms that make your average low interaction resource conversion puzzle so boring. Disastrous interface whit clashingly colourcoded iconographies smeared all over the place.

[Rating: 4/10] After several plays, the game is just average. The mechanisms all work together, and moving down the river is fun, but the overall experience is a bit meh. It feels very mechanical and there's a lot of counting and numbers to pay attention to, causing the game to feel almost unfinished. Played on bga so not moved by the golf foil on the board. Update: moving to a 4 as I've played the game several times now and don't want to play it again.

[Rating: 4/10] Run-of-the-mill game design. The lackluster use of the L5R world emphasizes it's another themeless Eurogame. FFG fails to impress me positively, again.

[Rating: 4/10] Player tokens are 4 different colors & building types are 4 different colors. Now imagine them mish-mashed together once the buildings are constructed along the river. Its just way too busy and gets difficult to tell which ones are yours, which are other player's etc. No matter how gorgeous the river itself looks, the graphic design has too many things visually competing for your attention making the board look crowded and confusing.
